newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore credit growth strong despite slowdown.
newsitem.headline: Singapore credit growth strong despite slowdown.

text.p: Singapore bank credit is continuing to grow in double digits despite the recent slowdown in the island's manufacturing sector, economists said on Monday.
Total bank loans rose 17 percent year-on-year in August to S$122.50 billion (US$86.88 billion), the Monetary Authority of Singapore said in its monthly report.

The credit expansion was slightly slower than the 18 percent year-on-year growth registered in July, but loans to the manufacturing, transport and building and construction sectors continued to be buoyant, rising by one percentage point each.
"Domestic bank loans are still firm mainly because of the robust construction sector," said Eddie Lee, regional economist with Vickers Ballas Securities.
Dealers said the figures supported the view that the current downturn in Singapore's manufacturing sector was cyclical and likely to be short-lived.

Local economists have mostly cut their third quarter forecasts for Singapore gross domestic product after last week's release of industrial production data for August, which showed manufacturing output fell 7.6 percent year-on-year.
A recent poll by the Business Times showed economists expected third quarter growth to be an average of 3.4 percent, 1.2 percentage points lower than their forecasts in September.
Singapore GDP growth for the first half of the year was 8.9 percent.
The manufacturing slowdown is mainly due to a slump in the electronics industry, which accounts for about half Singapore's total industrial output and 60 percent of its non-oil exports.
But the latest MAS figures show no drop in demand for credit for the key building and construction industry. Loans to this sector rose 32 percent in August, the MAS said.
Offshore loans by Singapore-based banks also picked up in August. U.S. dollar loans to non-bank customers grew by 6.5 percent in August against 1.3 percent the previous month.
"The pick-up in the Asian dollar market is also very encouraging especially after (it shrank) in June," said Lee.

UBS Securities said in a report published over the weekend that the Singapore manufacturing sector was experiencing its worst downturn since 1985. It said it expected Singapore's third quarter GDP growth to be just 1.9 percent.
But most economists said the latest MAS figures suggested there was no prospect of Singapore facing a real recession -- that is, three consecutive quarters of declining output.
The bank credit data is widely viewed as a leading indicator of growth between three and nine months in the future.
Most economists expect a pick-up in the fourth quarter, but full-year GDP growth is expected to fall below the government's projected range of 7.0 percent to 8.0 percent for 1996. ($1 = S$1.41)
